2e08dea7cc.why: Old issue fixed: the fourth choice is now in the parallel 'It is ... than they are' form and gives a reason, so all four choices are live (M1, the Sun is not a star). The key is true (NGSS 5-ESS1-1: brightness is down to distance). The new lure is truly wrong: the Sun is a star, the same kind of thing as the night-sky stars. 'Bigger' and 'hotter' stay wrong for the naked-eye stars (OpenStax 18.1). The stem never says the Sun is a star, so the new lure is not ruled out. No voice or grade problem.

444d79e2d5.why: Old issue fixed: the hat-brim picture is gone and the new fact (all four giants have rings) is in the stem. Grokipedia Ring_system confirms rings on all four giants. Jupiter's are 'a faint, dusty halo' that Earth telescopes never saw before Voyager 1. Uranus's are very dark (albedo under 0.05) and were found by occultation. Neptune's are 'faint and narrow'. Only Saturn's show in a small telescope (timeanddate, Florida SC.5.E.5.2). The rings' edge-on years (2025) do not make the general fact false. The context is accurate. Exactly one answer, and no tell.

8df372dcea.why: Old issue fixed: the lures are now real 5th-grade mix-ups (only Earth has a moon, gravity only on Earth, M10) in place of three landforms. Each lure is truly wrong. Mars has Phobos and Deimos and the outer planets have large moon systems (Grokipedia Natural_satellite). Everything with mass has gravity (NASA Space Place). Mars has water-ice and CO2-ice clouds (Grokipedia Climate_of_Mars), and Venus and Jupiter have clouds too. Key true (NASA). The context's claims all check out. 'Known to have' is the needed hedge, not a tell.

00c04492bd.why: Old issue fixed: the dead heat lure is replaced by 'Earth's gravity', so gravity appears twice and the student must know whose pull it is. The string picture has moved to the context. Naming Mars keeps 'Earth's gravity' live and wrong, since Earth's pull on Mars is negligible and the Sun holds the planets (NASA: 'Its gravity holds the solar system together'; Grokipedia Orbit). Magnetism and the planet's own spin are wrong. The context is accurate. Minor, not failing: the key is the one choice that shares a word with two others ('Sun's', 'gravity'), a convergence cue few 5th graders use.

b0a279ddb1.why: Old issue fixed: 'Ten years' is replaced by 'One season', so all four choices are 'One ___' and live. The key is true (NASA 365.25 days). The context's claims check out: a day is one spin (the grade-level simplification), a month is roughly one lunar orbit, and in the four-season model each season lasts about three months (Grokipedia Season). The fact sits at the floor of grade 5, as the judge accepted; no new problem.
